Notice the mix: cooking, storing, working and resting shared the same space. The word palace is a label from archaeologists, not a description of luxury. guion_largo.texto:
A palace is not always a place of luxury. In Xochicalco, the one the INAH calls the Palace has a more practical air.

According to the INAH, the Palace is on the middle level of the city. It is a complex of rooms, kitchens, workshops, storerooms and a temazcal, organized around courtyards.

A temazcal is a steam bath. It was used to cleanse the body and also in ceremonies. According to Andrews and Glascock, there were temazcales in the Acropolis and in the northern sector. That is why you will see one also in [the northern complex](xoc_20_agua_ritual_norte).

Medina Romero mentions that this palace and the La Malinche complex form a residential complex south of the city.

Think about that mix of spaces. Cooking, storing, working and resting were together, around one courtyard. It is rather a complex where people lived, cooked and worked.

This does not mean it was a palace like that of a European king. The word palace is a label from archaeologists. What the remains show are rooms, courtyards and work areas.

To understand where the rulers lived, you have to climb to [the Acropolis](xoc_17_acropolis). There stood, according to Hirth, the ruler’s palace and the city’s administrative center.

For now, take in the courtyards with your eyes and count how many rooms open onto each one.

texto: Count the courtyards you can see
Look for the spaces that could have been kitchens or storerooms
Imagine who worked and who slept in each room

texto.Spaces: rooms, kitchens, workshops, storerooms and temazcal, around courtyards
texto.Residential complex: with La Malinche, south of the city, according to Medina Romero

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Palace was the ruler’s house.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It is the name archaeologists give to a complex of rooms, kitchens, workshops and storerooms. The ruler’s residence is associated with the Acropolis.
